title: What is SBI?
text:
In many scientific disciplines it is commonplace to build simulations of natural systems due to the flexibility of general software compared to precisely defined sets of equations. However, these systems typically do not provide tractable likelihoods making parameter inference challenging. Simulation-based inference (SBI) encompasses many approximate inference techniques to overcome this issue, howerver in recent years SBI has been dominated by approaches that employ neural networks.
Most of these methods can be described as either amortising the likelihood (Neural Likelihood Estimation), the likelihood-ratio (Neural Ratio Estimation) or the posterior (Neural Posterior Estimation).



Overview of NLE, NRE and NPE. Taken from Cranmer et. al. 2020.


In brief, NLE fits a neural network with a tractable likelihood to simulated data, NRE learns \(\frac{p(x|\theta)}{p(\theta)}\) typically through a classifier or contrastive loss and NPE learns to perform posterior inference for a given simulator and prior in a single forward pass. Unlike NPE, NLE and NRE must be substituted into inference pipelines (e.g. MCMC, Variational Inference) every time a new inference is required.
In Metis we don’t aim to support every SBI use-case, but as our existing Normalising Flow surrogates have tractable likelihoods they can serve as NLE models.






Tip



If you intend to use a surrogate in an SBI inference pipeline ensure that the prior’s support is contained in the proposal/sampling distribution used to generate your data.

title: Normalising Flow
text: The normalising flow model is a stochastic surrogate with efficiently computable exact density.

title: Normalising Flow
section: When this might be a good fit
text:
When this might be a good fit
The normalising flow surrogate is a good option when stochasticity and/or evaluating the exact density of the surrogate is needed. Access to this density enables the surrogate to be used in parameter inference pipelines like MCMC, Variational Inference or Simulation-Based Inference (SBI).
Architecturally it is impelemented as a Transformer Autoregressive Flow (TARFlow), which is a modern normalising flow design that composes transformer blocks into an end-to-end invertible architecture. Its typical training cost is somewhere between the transformer surrogate and the flow matching model and its inference cost is similar to the flow matching model. Currently it only supports static inputs but we plan on implementing sequence conditioning as well.

title: Normalising Flow
text:
How Normalising Flows work

Maximum likelihood via change of variables
A Normalising Flow parametrises an invertible transformation \(f_{\theta}\) from the data distribution \(p_{\mathrm{data}}\) to a noise distribution \(p_0\) (usually Gaussian). Once trained the network can be inverted to transform noise samples into data. This transformation also has an associated density \(p_{\mathrm{model}}\) which is accessible via the change of variable formula
\[
\log p_{\mathrm{model}}(x)=\log p_0(f_{\theta}(x))+\log\vert\mathrm{det}(\frac{df_{\theta}(x)}{dx})\vert
\]
Architecturally Normalising Flows are designed to be exactly invertible with log-determinants that can be efficiently computed. This allows a maximum likelihood estimation objective to be implemented as
\[
\min_{\theta}\; -\log p_0(f_{\theta}(x))-\log\vert\mathrm{det}(\frac{df_{\theta}(x)}{dx})\vert
\]


Architecture
Normalising Flows have a rich literature with architectures that make different tradeoffs and until recently they were not regarded as scalable as generative models. Recently, the Transformer Autoregressive Flow (TARFlow) (Zhai et al. 2025) has emerged as a scalable approach to Normalising Flows. Like many Normalising Flows the overall network \(f_{\theta}\) is a composition of several invertible blocks \(f_{M}\circ f_{M-1}\cdots\circ f_{1}\). Each of these blocks flips the order of the sequence with \(\pi(x)\), and predicts scale \(\alpha\) and shift \(\mu\) parameters for each of the elements in the sequence with an autoregressive transformer \(T(x)\): \[
\begin{align}
&x^{\mathrm{output}}_{i}=(x^{\mathrm{input}}_{i}-\mu_{i})\odot \exp (-\alpha_i)\\
&\text{where } \mu_i \text{ and } \alpha_i \text{ are predicted by } T(x_{<i})\\
\end{align}
\]






Figure 1: Transformer Autoregressive Flow Block. Adapted from Zhai et al. (2025).



Crucially, since the transformer is causal, \(\alpha_i\) and \(\mu_i\) only depend on the elements strictly proceeding \(i\). Hence, the block can be exactly inverted by autoregressively rolling out
\[
x^{\mathrm{input}}_{i}=(x^{\mathrm{output}}_{i}\odot\exp(\alpha_i))+\mu_i
\]






Warning



Normalising Flows are known to struggle with numerical issues on high dimensional data like images. To overcome this, Zhai et al. (2025) train on noise-augmented data, and apply Tweedie’s trick to produce clean samples at inference. The downside of this approach is substantially more expensive inference and the loss of exact density evaluation.
In Metis we have not implemented this as we have not encountered this issue in testing on timeseries data from two malaria simulators.

title: MLP
text: The MLP (MultiLayer Perceptron) or feedforward neural network is Metis’s most basic architecture.

title: MLP
section: When this might be a good fit
text:
When this might be a good fit
The MLP is a good starting point for datasets with only static inputs. It is very fast to train and generate predictions from. It will likely not outperform the other architectures (when properly tuned), and unlike the Normalising Flow or Flow Matching architectures, the MLP is a deterministc surrogate.

title: MLP
text:
How does an MLP work?

Architectural walkthrough
An MLP’s computation is a series of matrix multiplications composed with non-linear activations. Metis’s implementation also includes residual connections which stablise the training of deeper networks.
In order to get a better sense of how these components work lets trace through the network’s forward computation:
x = self.input_layer(inputs)
for block in self.blocks:
    x = block(x)
x = self.output_layer(x)
The input_layer linearly projects (i.e. a matrix multiplication) the static input vector to vectors the size of the model’s hidden dimension. Next, we iteratively pass our transformed inputs through a series of residual blocks.
Each residual block applies several layers to the input and adds the result back to the original input:





flowchart LR
    x[x] --> layer1[Linear]
    layer1 --> activation1[ReLU]
    activation1 --> dots[...]
    dots --> layerN[Linear]
    x --> add["\+"]
    layerN --> add
    add --> out[output]


 Residual block structure. 



Finally, the output layer linearly projects x to the output dimensionality.


Training
The MLP is trained to minimise the Mean-Squared Error:
\[
\mathrm{Loss} = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}(\mathrm{MLP}^{\theta}(\mathrm{static\_input}_m)-\mathrm{output}_m)^2
\]

title: MLP
text:
Configuring an MLP
The MLP’s architecture is configured via:

input_dim: The number of static inputs.
output_dim: The flattened dimensionality of the sequence. (e.g. 5 timesteps where each step has 3 values would have a flat dim of 15)
num_blocks: The number of residual blocks in the network (i.e. network depth)
hidden_dim: The width of the network (all the matrices inside residual blocks will be \(\mathrm{hidden\_dim}\times \mathrm{hidden\_dim}\))
num_layers_per_block: The number of layers within a residual block (also controls depth)

The first two options are automatically configured for the dataset that you train on.

title: Transformer
text: The autoregressive transformer model is a flexible and deterministic surrogate.

title: Transformer
section: When this might be a good fit
text:
When this might be a good fit
The transformer is a great option when a deterministic surrogate suffices. Furthermore, it is more flexible than an MLP, supporting conditioning on both static inputs and sequences. Additionally, because it is autoregressive it naturally supports variable length outputs and starting generation from a variable number of observed datapoints.
Unfortunately, Transformer surrogates are slower to train and infer with and often require more tuning to match the performance of an MLP. However, they tend to benefit more from scaling data or the size of the network.

title: Transformer
text:
How transformers work

Architectural walkthrough
The transformer architecture is substantially more complex than an MLP’s so we won’t cover it in great depth here.
The most important part of the Transformer architecture is the self-attention mechansim which enables the model to process sequence data in a highly expressive way. In an attention computation, the entries of an incoming sequence \(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n\) are given corresponding query, key and value vectors via projection matrices (e.g. \(q_1=W_{q}x_1^T\)). These entries are collected in a \(Q\) (query), \(K\) (key) and \(V\) (value) matrix and the transformed sequence is computed via \(y=\mathrm{softmax}(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d}})V\). In an autoregressive transformer this computation is restricted so that query vectors may only attend to key vectors from the past:






Figure 1: Causal self-attention: each input may attend to itself and earlier inputs, but not future inputs.









Note



In practice multi-head attention is used, where models have several projection matrices and perform attention over the different sets of projections independently and in parallel and then combine the results.






Figure 2: Multi-head attention: Each block is a projected sequence of query, key, or value vectors.





During training the attention computation can be done over entire sequences at once (this is a major strength of the transformer), however, during inference, the sequence is iteratively generated. Since the latest entry in the sequence still needs to attend to every entry that came before it we are forced to either repeatedly recompute prior key and value vectors or to store them in a Key-Value Cache (KV-Cache). For larger transformers or generating longer sequences using a KV-Cache can significantly speed up inference.
In Metis we also support options like interleaving full self-attention with sliding window attention which halves the maximum size of the attention window for a computational speedup:






Figure 3: Sliding window self-attention: Later tokens may not attend to the furtherest tokens in the past.



We additionally support specifying fewer key-value heads (i.e. projections) than query heads to make attention more efficient and reduce the size of the KV-cache. This is known as Grouped-Query Attention.






Figure 4: Grouped-query attention: Multiple query heads share each key-value head.






Training
Language transformers train with Cross-Entropy Loss over tokens but since our data is typically continuous, we use a next-token MSE loss.

title: Motivating surrogate modelling
text:
Many scientific disciplines are increasingly reliant on computational simulators which reproduce complex behaviours. However, these simulators are often slow and expensive to run, rendering tasks like scenario analysis, forecasting and parameter inference, difficult or otherwise impractical. For example, its been reported that a single forward simulation over a large COVID-19 Agent-Based Model like JUNE can take several days (Chopra et al. 2023). Surrogate models serve as cost-effective approximations of these systems. Whilst surrogates have been implemented with techniques like nonparametric statistical methods and splines, modern neural network approaches offer significantly greater flexibility and are often more performant.






Tip



For an overview of the surrogate modelling process and a reporting standard for surrogates, see SMRS (Semenova et al. 2025).

title: Motivating surrogate modelling
text:
Introducing METIS
METIS is a set of configurable recipes for training neural surrogates of time series simulators. METIS implements several neural network architectures and algorithms and is designed so that practictioners can easily train and sweep over different combinations purely through simple config files and comandline overrrides. Using METIS to develop surrogates for existing simulators simply requires preparing data in the correct format and supplying appropriate config files.







Important



METIS is designed to be useful to those without deep learning expertise, however, it will be beneficial to have some basic familiarity with neural networks and their training. If you’re unfamiliar or feeling a bit rusty these resources should be helpful:

title: Saving and Loading models
text:
Once trained, we’d like to deploy our models in some downstream applications. We may also want to resume a training run that was interrupted (e.g. due to a hardware issue) or simply continue training if model performance was still improving.


Both of these use cases are addressed via Metis’s ‘checkpointing’ system. The checkpointer saves the model weights, current training step, pseudo-random generator states and the optimiser (amongst other things) so that training may be resumed seamlessly.
To enable checkpointing in your run simply set how often you’d like a checkpoint saved (number of steps)
checkpointer:
  save_every: 1000
And to continue training from an existing checkpoint we set resume_from,
checkpointer:
  resume_from: outputs/example_run/checkpoint



In order to load just the model weights in a script we first instantiate the model and then load the weights into the model via
ckpt = torch.load(path_to_checkpoint.ckpt, map_location='cpu', weights_only=False)
model.load_state_dict(ckpt['model'])

text: The entrypoint to a training job in Metis is train.py. Rather than importing training code or writing a script, in Metis we simply run train.py in the terminal or a notebook with the appropriate config files supplied. Given the data and config file we prepared earlier, getting started with training is a matter of overriding the default data config.

title: Training in METIS
text:
Overriding the default training config
First we ensure the repository root is our current directory since this is where train.py is located.

import os
from IPython.display import Image

if os.path.basename(os.getcwd()) == "examples":
    os.chdir("..")
print("cwd:", os.getcwd())

Now we’ll override the default training config to use our sirds dataset and in order to check that our model fit the data well we will generate some samples via the sampling arguments:

sampling.generate_samples=True indicates we’d like the surrogate to generate samples once we’re done training
sampling.samples_name specifies where we would like the samples saved
sample.subsample used to generate samples for only a subset of the validation set

Now go ahead and run this:

uv run train.py \
  --config-name default \
  dataset=sirds \
  sampling.generate_samples=True \
  sampling.samples_name=examples/mlp_plot.png \
  sampling.subsample=5

title: Example SIRDS model
text: We use a stochastic SIRDS (Susceptible–Infected–Recovered–Dead–Susceptible) compartmental model as a running example throughout the docs. The particulars of how this model work aren’t too important, but the basic idea is that our simulator depends on some static input parameters (I0, beta, etc…) and produces stochastic timeseries of compartment counts over time.
crumbs: Basics of surrogate modelling with Metis

title: Example SIRDS model
text:
Code definition


import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def simulate_sirds(
    I0=0.005, beta=0.4, gamma=0.1, omega=0.02, mu=0.01, T=365, dt=1.0, N=1000, seed=None
):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n = int(T / dt) + 1
    I0_count = max(0, min(N, int(round(I0 * N))))

    S = np.zeros(n, dtype=np.int32)
    I = np.zeros(n, dtype=np.int32)
    R = np.zeros(n, dtype=np.int32)
    D = np.zeros(n, dtype=np.int32)
    S[0], I[0], R[0], D[0] = N - I0_count, I0_count, 0, 0

    for k in range(n - 1):
        p_inf = 1.0 - np.exp(-beta * I[k] / N * dt)
        p_rec = 1.0 - np.exp(-gamma * dt)
        p_die = 1.0 - np.exp(-mu * dt)
        p_sus = 1.0 - np.exp(-omega * dt)

        new_I = rng.binomial(S[k], p_inf)

        # Competing risks: each infected individual can recover, die, or stay infected.
        # Use a multinomial draw so recovery + death never exceeds I[k].
        p_stay = max(0.0, 1.0 - p_rec - p_die)
        outcomes = rng.multinomial(I[k], [p_rec, p_die, p_stay])
        new_R = outcomes[0]
        new_D = outcomes[1]

        new_S = rng.binomial(R[k], p_sus)

        S[k + 1] = S[k] - new_I + new_S
        I[k + 1] = I[k] + new_I - new_R - new_D
        R[k + 1] = R[k] + new_R - new_S
        D[k + 1] = D[k] + new_D

    return S, I, R, D

title: Example SIRDS model
text:
Example realisations
Here we again emphasise that even with fixed input parameters, varying the random seed produces different realisations.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(10, 4.5))
for s in range(20):
    S, I, R, D = simulate_sirds(seed=s)
    t = np.arange(len(S))
    ax.plot(t, S, color="#2E86AB", label="S" if s == 0 else None, alpha=0.35, lw=1)
    ax.plot(t, I, color="#C73E1D", label="I" if s == 0 else None, alpha=0.35, lw=1)
    ax.plot(t, R, color="#6A994E", label="R" if s == 0 else None, alpha=0.35, lw=1)
    ax.plot(t, D, color="#C21B8A", label="D" if s == 0 else None, alpha=0.35, lw=1)
ax.set(
    xlabel="time (days)",
    ylabel="count",
    title="",
)
ax.legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Why sweep?
text:
The quality of a model is determined not only by its learning algorithm and data but also by hyperparameters which control the architecture or aspects of the learning algorithm. Models are often quite sensitive to these hyperparameters and so sweeping or tuning hyperparameters can lead to substantial performance improvemnents (or in some cases may be required to successfully train a model at all).
Given that large neural networks can memorise their training data given sufficient training steps, it is important to maintain held-out i.i.d. data so that the model’s ability to generalise beyond its training data can be assessed. Generally this entails partitioning datasets into a training set and a tuning set, with the majority of the data being allocated to the training set. Usually great care is taken to ensure that these sets are identically distributed without information about the tuning set being leaked in the training set. In Metis our dataloader automatically partitions datasets into train and tune by the parameter group, ensuring that all the realistions in a group are in one of the sets.

title: Why sweep?
text:
Basic sweeping
The basic hyperparameter sweep workflow is:

Choose hyperparameters to fix (e.g. batch size) and sweep over (e.g. learning rate)
Choose the metric you’d like to target
Define how you’d like to sample the sweep space (e.g. random, bayesian optimisation) and the number of training runs you’d like to do
Launch one or more sweep agents
Analyze sweep results and (if necessecary) launch another more targeted sweep

Over the next few tutorials we’ll see how to use tools like Weights & Biases to manage sweeps and a walkthrough of how sweeping works in Metis.

title: METIS sweep config
text:
In this walkthrough we’ll see how to setup a sweep for an MLP model on our SIRDS dataset. As with training, sweeps in Metis are driven through a config.


For this walkthrough we’ll focus on sweeping over the peak_lr, the lr_warmup_frac, the number of model blocks, and the hidden dimension of the model. We’ll keep batch size, layers per block and the maximum number of steps fixed.






Tip



If you’re only going to sweep over one or two hyperparameters prioritise the peak_lr and lr_warmup_frac. They often have an outsized effect on model performance.





The most common metric to optimise is validation loss, however in some applications other metrics might be targeted. In Metis we default to targeting the final validation loss of our models (final_val_loss).



Weights & Biases support sweeping strategies like grid where every single possibile combination of hyperparameters in the config is systemtically explored, random which just randomly samples from the possibile configurations and bayes which uses Bayesian optimisation to intelligently select the next sweep experiments. In this tutorial we’ll stick to bayes.
Additionally, you have a choice of specifying the options for each hyperparameter as a fixed list, or with a sampling distribution over a certain range:
  #Params to optimise
  peak_lr:
    min: 0.000001
    max: 0.01 
    distribution: log_uniform_values #log uniform sampling of [1e-6,1e-2] 
  lr_warmup_frac: 
    values: [0.0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4] #fixed
  model.num_blocks: 
    min: 5
    max: 20
    distribution: int_uniform # compact way of writing [5,6,...,20]
  model.hidden_dim: 
    values: [128, 256, 512, 1024] #Fixed set of options
We don’t explicitly set the number of runs in the config but its useful to decide this early on since with a smaller budget of experiments its likely better to keep your sampling strategy more focused. For this demo we’ll plan on doing 50 runs.
Putting everything together our sweep config looks like:
program: train
project: your_existing_weights_and_biases_project
metric:
  name: final_val_loss
  goal: minimize

method: bayes
parameters:
  #Fixed
  sampling.generate_samples:
    value: false #don't generate samples during sweeping
  dataset: 
    value: sirds
  plot_loss_curves:
    value: false #don't make unnecessary plots
  model:
    value: mlp_default #we'll modify mlp default
  logger.use_wandb:
    value: true #essential
  logger.tags:
    value: [mlp, sirds]
  batch_size:
    value: 128
  max_steps:
   value: 2000
  
  #Params to optimise
  peak_lr:
    min: 0.000001
    max: 0.01 
    distribution: log_uniform_values
  lr_warmup_frac: 
    values: [0.0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4]

title: METIS sweep config
text:
In this walkthrough we’ll see how to setup a sweep for an MLP model on our SIRDS dataset. As with training, sweeps in Metis are driven through a config.


For this walkthrough we’ll focus on sweeping over the peak_lr, the lr_warmup_frac, the number of model blocks, and the hidden dimension of the model. We’ll keep batch size, layers per block and the maximum number of steps fixed.






Tip



If you’re only going to sweep over one or two hyperparameters prioritise the peak_lr and lr_warmup_frac. They often have an outsized effect on model performance.





The most common metric to optimise is validation loss, however in some applications other metrics might be targeted. In Metis we default to targeting the final validation loss of our models (final_val_loss).



Weights & Biases support sweeping strategies like grid where every single possibile combination of hyperparameters in the config is systemtically explored, random which just randomly samples from the possibile configurations and bayes which uses Bayesian optimisation to intelligently select the next sweep experiments. In this tutorial we’ll stick to bayes.
Additionally, you have a choice of specifying the options for each hyperparameter as a fixed list, or with a sampling distribution over a certain range:
  #Params to optimise
  peak_lr:
    min: 0.000001
    max: 0.01 
    distribution: log_uniform_values #log uniform sampling of [1e-6,1e-2] 
  lr_warmup_frac: 
    values: [0.0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4] #fixed
  model.num_blocks: 
    min: 5
    max: 20
    distribution: int_uniform # compact way of writing [5,6,...,20]
  model.hidden_dim: 
    values: [128, 256, 512, 1024] #Fixed set of options
We don’t explicitly set the number of runs in the config but its useful to decide this early on since with a smaller budget of experiments its likely better to keep your sampling strategy more focused. For this demo we’ll plan on doing 50 runs.
Putting everything together our sweep config looks like:
program: train
project: your_existing_weights_and_biases_project
metric:
  name: final_val_loss
  goal: minimize

method: bayes
parameters:
  #Fixed
  sampling.generate_samples:
    value: false #don't generate samples during sweeping
  dataset: 
    value: sirds
  plot_loss_curves:
    value: false #don't make unnecessary plots
  model:
    value: mlp_default #we'll modify mlp default
  logger.use_wandb:
    value: true #essential
  logger.tags:
    value: [mlp, sirds]
  batch_size:
    value: 128
  max_steps:
   value: 2000
  
  #Params to optimise
  peak_lr:
    min: 0.000001
    max: 0.01 
    distribution: log_uniform_values
  lr_warmup_frac: 
    values: [0.0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4]
  model.num_blocks: 
    min: 5
    max: 20
    distribution: int_uniform
  model.hidden_dim: 
    values: [128, 256, 512, 1024]

command:
- ${env}
- ${interpreter}
- "-m"
- ${program}
- "--config-name"
- "default"
#These hydra options disable the creation of
#output folders for all the runs
- "hydra.output_subdir=null"
- "hydra/job_logging=disabled"
- "hydra/hydra_logging=disabled"
- "hydra.run.dir=."
- ${args_no_hyphens}
Save this to configs/sweep/sirds/mlp.yaml. Now we’re ready to register our sweep with Weights & Biases:
uv run wandb sweep --project your_existing_weights_and_biases_project configs/sweep/sirds/mlp.yaml
This will output a string of the form <entity>/<project-name>/<sweep-id> that we’ll give to weights and biases agents when launching sweeps.

title: Weights & Biases
text:
Weights & Biases is a platform for manage sweeps and tracking experiments. At a basic level it can be used to track the progress of your training runs and to serve as a record of experiments you’ve done. For regular training runs this can be enabled by setting these options in a training config:
logger:
  use_wandb: true
  project: your_existing_weights_and_biases_project
  tags: [] #any tags you'd like to apply to the run for organisation






Tip



You’ll need to make a free Weights and Biases account if you don’t have one.


Here’s an example of the sort of information you can get at a glance:



Screenshot of a Weights & Biases dashboard for a Metis training run


Once launched, Weights & Biases collects all the runs in a sweep together, allows you to sort the runs by key metrics (e.g. final validation loss) and computes things like hyperparameter correlation with validation loss:



Screenshot of a Weights & Biases parameter correlation for a sweep


For more advanced use cases its also possible to download the raw results for local analysis.

title: Training on multiple GPUs
text:
Common forms of parallelism during training. Taken from Raschka (2023)
Metis can take advantage of multiple GPUs located in the same machine via data parallelism, wherein indentical copies of the model on separate GPUs are fed with different batches of data, their gradients aggregated and the overall parameter update copied to each GPU. Whilst more sophisticated forms of parallelism are possible, and often required at larger scales, we do not support them due to the complexity they introduce.

title: Training on multiple GPUs
text:
From one to four GPUs
Recall our usual single-GPU command,
uv run train.py --config-name default dataset=sirds
To use four GPUs on one machine, set num_gpus:
uv run train.py --config-name default dataset=sirds num_gpus=4
train.py starts one worker process per GPU itself, so everything else (Hydra output directories, checkpoints, wandb logging, --multirun sweeps) works exactly as it does on one GPU.
In cases where you want to use only a subset of the GPUs, the CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable can be used to restrict the GPUs visible to train.py. For example, to train on only GPUs 2 and 3:
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=2,3 uv run train.py --config-name default dataset=sirds num_gpus=2

title: Training on multiple GPUs
text:
Batch size
batch_size is the global batch size across all GPUs. It must be divisible by num_gpus. For example, batch_size=128 with four GPUs gives each GPU 32 samples per optimizer step.

title: Training on multiple GPUs
text:
Troubleshooting
Common checks when a job fails to start:

Confirm nvidia-smi lists at least num_gpus visible GPUs.
Confirm batch_size is divisible by num_gpus.
Set NCCL_DEBUG=INFO before the command when diagnosing NCCL initialization or communication failures.

text: METIS is configured end-to-end with the Hydra. You don’t need to touch Python to change models, datasets or training settings — you compose and override Hydra configs instead.

title: Hydra crash course
text:
Hydra basics
Hydra’s configuration files are simple text-based YAML files. For example a basic training config might look like this:
data: malaria_data
model: transformer
steps: 10000
Once ingested into a Python program (omitted here) the config’s values can be accessed like any object:
print(config.steps) #should print 10000
Importantly, an entry’s value doesn’t have to just be a string or a number, it can refer to another configuration file. For example, we could create a configuration file for each dataset that stores where the data lives and other metadata like the column names.
├── configs/
│   ├── config.yaml
│   ├── data
│       ├── malaria_data.yaml
│       └── ebola_data.yaml
│   
└── my_program.py
Then malaria_data.yaml might contain something like
data_path: datasets/malaria_simulations.parquet
column_names:
 - a
 - b
 - c
Then to get Hydra to use this config instead of a string we use the defaults list directive:
defaults:
  data: malaria_data

model: transformer
steps: 10000
defaults is a special directive telling Hydra to use data/malaria_data.yaml when composing the configuration object. The resulting object is a composition of configs from defaults with configs specified in your config.yaml.
Furthermore, when running our program in the commandline, we can override configs or values without modifying the config file itself:
uv run my_program --config-name config data=ebola_data steps=5000
Finally, overrides can happen inside configs themselves, for example, a particular training run might fetch the data from a different location but still have the same column names as the default malaria_data.yaml:
defaults:
  - data: malaria_data #start off with the usual values in malaria_data.yaml
  - _self_ #apply overrides in this config last 

data:
  data_path: new_location #override the data config's data_path
model: transformer
steps: 10000
These core features allow us to keep our configuration files nicely structured and make it quick to try different models or datasets.






Tip



Hydra has many more features not mentioned here. If you ever get stuck or feel a bit lost the Hydra tutorials are excellent and most LLMs are helpful when writing or editing Hydra configs.

Here’s the completed config for our example SIRDS dataset. It’s fairly self-explanatory, surrogate_input_variables are static input values that we’d like our surrogate to condition on and output_variables are what we’d like the surrogate to predict. grouping_variables are used to group reps together, for most use-cases grouping_variables should be the same as the surrogate_inputs, but for some datasets this flexibility is needed.

path: examples/sirds_data.parquet

exclude_output_variables: null

title: Walkthrough: Preparing data for METIS
text:
Multiple SIRDS realisations
For the SIRDS simulator we also need to store the simulator’s inputs and disambiguate between different realisations with the same inputs. Simulator inputs are just treated as another column, and different realisations are disambiguated via the ‘rep’ column:


Code
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


def simulate_sirds(
    I0=0.005, beta=0.4, gamma=0.1, omega=0.02, mu=0.01, T=365, dt=1.0, N=1000, seed=None
):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n = int(T / dt) + 1
    I0_count = max(0, min(N, int(round(I0 * N))))

    S = np.zeros(n, dtype=np.int32)
    I = np.zeros(n, dtype=np.int32)
    R = np.zeros(n, dtype=np.int32)
    D = np.zeros(n, dtype=np.int32)
    S[0], I[0], R[0], D[0] = N - I0_count, I0_count, 0, 0

    for k in range(n - 1):
        p_inf = 1.0 - np.exp(-beta * I[k] / N * dt)
        p_rec = 1.0 - np.exp(-gamma * dt)
        p_die = 1.0 - np.exp(-mu * dt)
        p_sus = 1.0 - np.exp(-omega * dt)

        new_I = rng.binomial(S[k], p_inf)

        # Competing risks: each infected individual can recover, die, or stay infected.
        # Use a multinomial draw so recovery + death never exceeds I[k].
        p_stay = max(0.0, 1.0 - p_rec - p_die)
        outcomes = rng.multinomial(I[k], [p_rec, p_die, p_stay])
        new_R = outcomes[0]
        new_D = outcomes[1]

        new_S = rng.binomial(R[k], p_sus)

        S[k + 1] = S[k] - new_I + new_S
        I[k + 1] = I[k] + new_I - new_R - new_D
        R[k + 1] = R[k] + new_R - new_S
        D[k + 1] = D[k] + new_D

    return S, I, R, D



# the simulator inputs
params = dict(I0=0.005, beta=0.4, gamma=0.1, omega=0.02, mu=0.01)

# number of realisations we would like 
n_reps = 5
 
frames = []
for rep in range(n_reps):
    
    S, I, R, D = simulate_sirds(seed=rep, **params, T=100)
    S,I,R,D=S[1:],I[1:],R[1:], D[1:] # we drop t=0 since for this simulator it carries no information
    t = np.arange(len(S))
    frames.append(pd.DataFrame({
        "rep": rep,
        "t": t,
        "I_t": I,
        "S_t": S,
        "R_t": R,
        "I_0": params["I0"],
        "beta": params["beta"],
        "gamma": params["gamma"],
        "omega": params["omega"],
        "mu":params["mu"],
    }))
    df = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)

print(f"reps:  {df['rep'].unique()}")

text:
Sampling the parameter space
When building a dataset of simulator realisations its important to consider which regions of the simulator’s parameter (or input) space you sample and how they are sampled. For example, a simulator may be more sensitive in a certain parameter region or parameters physically constrained to lie within a particular range. For our example we will simply sample uniformly within reasonable ranges but another popular approach is Latin Hypercube Sampling (see Scipy Latin Hypercube).


import seaborn as sns

N_PARAMS = 1_000

# reproducible parameter sampling
param_rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
I0_vals = param_rng.uniform(0.01, 0.1, N_PARAMS)
beta_vals = param_rng.uniform(0.10, 0.80, N_PARAMS)
gamma_vals = param_rng.uniform(0.05, 0.30, N_PARAMS)
omega_vals = param_rng.uniform(0.005, 0.05, N_PARAMS)
mu_vals = param_rng.uniform(0.005, 0.05, N_PARAMS)

#visualise the sampled space
sns.pairplot(
    pd.DataFrame({'I0':I0_vals, 'beta':beta_vals, 'gamma':gamma_vals, 'omega':omega_vals, 'mu':mu_vals}), corner=True,height=2
)

Creating the full dataset
Given our parameters we can now create an entire dataset.

import time
N_REPS = 5
T, DT = 200, 1.0
n_steps_sim = int(T / DT) + 1  # simulator produces this many steps including t=0
n_steps = n_steps_sim - 1  # we drop t=0 since it carries no information
total_rows = N_PARAMS * N_REPS * n_steps


# preallocate
t_template = np.arange(1, n_steps_sim) * DT
rep = np.empty(total_rows, dtype=np.int32)
t_col = np.empty(total_rows, dtype=np.float32)
I_col = np.empty(total_rows, dtype=np.int32)
S_col = np.empty(total_rows, dtype=np.int32)
R_col = np.empty(total_rows, dtype=np.int32)
D_col = np.empty(total_rows, dtype=np.int32)
I0_col = np.empty(total_rows, dtype=np.float32)
beta_col = np.empty(total_rows, dtype=np.float32)
gamma_col = np.empty(total_rows, dtype=np.float32)
omega_col = np.empty(total_rows, dtype=np.float32)
mu_col = np.empty(total_rows, dtype=np.float32)

print(f"Running {N_PARAMS} × {N_REPS} = {N_PARAMS * N_REPS} simulations...")
t0 = time.time()

row = 0
for i in range(N_PARAMS):
    params = dict(
        I0=I0_vals[i], beta=beta_vals[i], gamma=gamma_vals[i], omega=omega_vals[i], mu=mu_vals[i]
    )
    for r in range(N_REPS):
        seed = i * N_REPS + r  # unique across all runs
        S, I, R,D = simulate_sirds(seed=seed, T=T, dt=DT, **params)

        sl = slice(row, row + n_steps)
        rep[sl] = r + 1  # 1..5
        t_col[sl] = t_template
        I_col[sl] = I[1:]
        S_col[sl] = S[1:]
        R_col[sl] = R[1:]

        I0_col[sl] = params["I0"]
        beta_col[sl] = params["beta"]
        gamma_col[sl] = params["gamma"]
        omega_col[sl] = params["omega"]
        mu_col[sl] = params["mu"]
        row += n_steps

    if (i + 1) % 100 == 0:
        print(f"  {i + 1}/{N_PARAMS} inputs done ({time.time() - t0:.1f}s)")

title: METIS
text:
METIS is a collection of configurable “recipes” for training neural network surrogate (emulator) models that stand in for expensive stochastic simulators. Instead of running a slow simulator every time you need a sample, you train a model once and then generate realisations cheaply.
The codebase favours simple, single-file implementations wired together with Hydra configuration, so that you can swap models, datasets and training settings by editing YAML rather than code.

title: METIS
text:
How these docs are organised

Basics of surrogate modelling — what surrogate modelling is, the SIRDS example simulator, preparing data, a Hydra crash course, and training your first model.
Different kinds of surrogates — the model families on offer (MLP, Transformer, Flow Matching, Normalising Flow), when to reach for each, and how their configs work.
Utilities and advanced features — training on multiple GPUs and visualising datasets.
Sweeping — tuning hyperparameters with Weights & Biases and the METIS sweep configs.
SBI — using a trained surrogate for simulation-based inference.







Tip



New here? Start with Motivating surrogate modelling and work through the Basics section in order.

title: Flow Matching
text: The flow matching transformer model is a flexible and stochastic surrogate.

title: Flow Matching
section: When this might be a good fit
text:
When this might be a good fit
The flow matching surrogate is a good option when stochasticity is needed. Architecturally, it is implemented as a modified transformer and also supports static and sequence conditioning.

title: Flow Matching
text:
How flow matching works

Architecture
The flow matching surrogate is parametrised with a non-causal transformer that processes the entire sequence in parallel.


Flow Matching
Flow Matching and Diffusion models are the current state-of-the-art learning algorithms for continuous valued data (e.g. images, protein-structure prediction). In brief, these models learn time-varying velocity fields which can be used to transport a sample of pure noise (e.g. from a Gaussian) to the data distribution. In order to generate samples the time-varying velocity field \(v_{\theta}\) must be integrated over time \(t\) to transport a noise sample \(x_0\) to the data distribution: \[
x_{\mathrm{pred}} = x_0+\int_{t=0}^{t=1}v_{\theta}(x_t|c)dt\text{, where } c \text{ is conditioning (i.e. surrogate inputs)}
\]
In practice this is achieved via numerical ODE solvers like Euler or Heun, with the number of solver steps introducing a trade-off between speed and quality.






NoteTechnical note





Diffusion models have equivalent ODE and SDE forms and can be sampled via SDE-solvers like Euler-Maruyama or ODE-solvers like Heun. See Song et al. (2021).








Flow matching models iteratively transform samples from noise to the data distribution. Animation produced by Floor Eijkelboom.


By fixing the conditioning \(c\) and varying the initial noise, you can sample multiple realisations rather than the average realisation that an MLP or Autoregressive transformer learn.






Tip



The mathematical details of these models and the derivation of their training objectives are out of scope but if you’re interested you may find these resources helpful:

Accessible introduction to Diffusion (YouTube)
Introduction to Normalising Flows and Flow Matching (Blog)
Explanation of score-based diffusion by its inventor (Blog)
Unifying flow matching and diffusion (Monograph)

title: Flow Matching
text:
Configuring a Flow Matching model
Metis’s implementation is designed to support different kinds of Stochastic Interpolant algorithms (the general name for diffusion and flow matching), although currently only Flow Matching has been set up and tested. The top-level config controls details like the type of algorithm and solver steps for evaluation and contains an inner architectural config that is very similar to the transformer:

interpolant: Currently only ‘flow-matching’ supported.
num_steps: Number of ODE solver steps for evaluations, does not impact training.
solver: ODE solver, currently only ‘heun’ (second-order) and ‘euler’ (first-order) are supported.
multi_mode: Whether to generate multiple samples from the median of the parameter group (‘median’ option) or to generate multiple samples for each entry in the parameter group (‘entire_parameter_group’). This second option only makes sense for models like HRP and Magenta where realisations within the same parameter group can have different static inputs.
sit:

sequence_len: Number of timesteps in the data sequence.
data_dim: Number of variables per datapoint.
cond_dim: Number of static input variables.
n_blocks: Number of transfomer blocks.
n_head: Number of query heads in attention layers.
n_kv_head: Number of key-value heads in attention layers.
qkv_bias: Whether the projection matrices in the self-attention module use biases.
emdb_dim: Hidden dimension of the network
cond_dropout_prob: Currently unused - but could be used to enable classifier-free guidance
in_and_out_biases: Whether the input and out projections use learnable biases.
cross_attn: The cross attention config for sequence conditioning, can be None.


The sequence_len, data_dim and cond_dim are all automatically configured based on the dataset config.

title: VI and MCMC with iTarFlow
text: Metis’s Normalising Flow surrogate provides an exact likelihood, enabling us to use it in-place of our simulator/data-generating processes’s likelihood function in standard inference pipelines.

title: VI and MCMC with iTarFlow
text:
Setup
Run the commands from the repository root in a terminal, or download this page as a notebook into examples/ and run its cells. The setup cell below switches to the repository root. In a terminal, omit the notebook-only %%bash lines.

import os
from pathlib import Path

if Path.cwd().name == "examples":
    os.chdir("..")
print("cwd:", Path.cwd())

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from hydra.utils import instantiate
from IPython.display import Image
from omegaconf import OmegaConf

from dataloader import prepare_splits
from examples.sirds_simulator import simulate_sirds

DEVICE = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
torch.manual_seed(42)

title: VI and MCMC with iTarFlow
text:
Train the surrogate
As before, we’ll train our normalising flow (NF) surrogate on the SIRDS dataset we prepared:

%%bash
uv run train.py \
  --config-name default \
  model=itarflow_default \
  dataset=sirds \
  max_steps=10_000 \
  checkpointer.save_every=10_000 \
  hydra.run.dir=outputs/sbi-tutorial-nf \
  sampling.generate_samples=True \
  sampling.samples_name=examples/sbi_tutorial_nf_realisations.png \
  sampling.subsample=5

And visualise the surrogate’s realisations to ensure it has fit the data well.

Image(filename="examples/sbi_tutorial_nf_realisations.png")

title: VI and MCMC with iTarFlow
text:
Load the trained surrogate
The training command writes to outputs/sbi-tutorial-nf. We reconstruct the model from its saved configuration and load the final checkpoint.

run_dir = Path("outputs/sbi-tutorial-nf")
cfg = OmegaConf.load(run_dir / ".hydra/config.yaml")

# These dimensions are set from the dataset by the training pipeline.
cfg.model.out_channels = len(cfg.dataset.output_variables)
cfg.model.num_timesteps = cfg.dataset.num_timesteps
cfg.model.static_in = len(cfg.dataset.surrogate_input_variables)

nf = instantiate(cfg.model).to(DEVICE)
checkpoint = torch.load(
    run_dir / "checkpoints/last.pt",
    map_location="cpu",
    weights_only=False,
)
nf.load_state_dict(checkpoint["model"])
nf.eval()
nf.requires_grad_(False)

The checkpoint does not contain normalization statistics, so we reproduce them from the same dataset using the training pipeline’s preprocessing.

_, _, input_stats, output_stats = prepare_splits(
    cfg.dataset.path,
    0.1,
    42,
    cfg.dataset.grouping_variables,
    cfg.dataset.surrogate_input_variables,
    cfg.dataset.output_variables,
    cfg.dataset.num_timesteps,
    cfg.dataset.trunc_until,
    cfg.dataset.input_col_to_source_col,
)

# Static conditioning inputs use the statistics at the first timestep.
input_mean = input_stats.means[:, 0].to(DEVICE)
input_std = input_stats.stds[:, 0].to(DEVICE)

# iTarFlow uses (batch, time, channels).
series_mean = output_stats.means.T.to(DEVICE)
series_std = output_stats.stds.T.to(DEVICE)

title: VI and MCMC with iTarFlow
text:
Preparing an observation
For this tutorial we’ll generate our observation from our SIRDS simulator. We infer the initial infected fraction \(I_0\), beta, gamma and omega, treating only the mortality rate as known.

TRUE_I0 = 0.02
TRUE_BETA = 0.45
TRUE_GAMMA = 0.12
TRUE_OMEGA = 0.025
TRUE_MU = 0.01

S_obs, I_obs, R_obs, D_obs = simulate_sirds(
    I0=TRUE_I0, beta=TRUE_BETA, gamma=TRUE_GAMMA, omega=TRUE_OMEGA,
    mu=TRUE_MU, T=cfg.dataset.num_timesteps, seed=999,
)
y_obs_raw = np.stack([S_obs, I_obs, R_obs, D_obs], axis=-1)[1:]  # drop t=0
y_obs = torch.as_tensor(y_obs_raw, dtype=torch.float32, device=DEVICE)
y_obs = ((y_obs - series_mean) / series_std).unsqueeze(0)

title: VI and MCMC with iTarFlow
text:
Choosing the prior
We’ll assume independent uniform priors: \[
\begin{align}
&I_0 \sim \mathcal{U}(0.01, 0.1)\\
&\beta \sim \mathcal{U}(0.2, 0.8)\\
&\gamma \sim \mathcal{U}(0.05, 0.3)\\
&\omega \sim \mathcal{U}(0.005, 0.05)
\end{align}
\]

title: VI and MCMC with iTarFlow
text:
The inference problem
Given our observation \(x'\), our choice of priors \(p(\theta)\) and our trained surrogate we have an unnormalised posterior density,
\[
p(\theta|x=x') \propto \hat{p}(x=x'|\theta)p(\theta)
\]
To obtain samples from the posterior we need to either fit a parametrised distribution or run MCMC.

title: VI and MCMC with iTarFlow
text:
Variational Inference
We introduce a parametrised distribution \(q_{\phi}\), in this case a multivariate Gaussian transformed to lie within the parameter bounds, and maximise the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO): \[
\max_{\phi}\;\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim q_{\phi}(\theta)}[\log \hat{p}(x=x'|\theta)] - \mathrm{KL}[q_{\phi}(\theta)\,\vert\vert\,p(\theta)]
\]






Note



This is equivalent to minimising the reverse KL-divergence between \(q_{\phi}\) and the posterior.


We implement this in code using PyTorch’s distributions module.

import math
import torch.nn.functional as F
import torch.distributions as dist

PARAM_BOUNDS = {
    "I_0": (0.01, 0.1),
    "beta": (0.2, 0.8),
    "gamma": (0.05, 0.3),
    "omega": (0.005, 0.05),
}
lo = torch.tensor([b[0] for b in PARAM_BOUNDS.values()], device=DEVICE)
hi = torch.tensor([b[1] for b in PARAM_BOUNDS.values()], device=DEVICE)

DATA_DIM = y_obs[0].numel()

n_params = len(PARAM_BOUNDS)
q_mu = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(n_params, device=DEVICE))
q_L_flat = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(n_params * (n_params + 1) // 2, device=DEVICE))

def build_q():
    L = torch.zeros(n_params, n_params, device=DEVICE)
    idx = torch.tril_indices(n_params, n_params, device=DEVICE)
    L[idx[0], idx[1]] = q_L_flat
    diag_idx = torch.arange(n_params, device=DEVICE)
    L[diag_idx, diag_idx] = F.softplus(L[diag_idx, diag_idx]) + 1e-4

    base = dist.MultivariateNormal(q_mu, scale_tril=L)
    transforms = [dist.SigmoidTransform(), dist.AffineTransform(loc=lo, scale=(hi - lo))]
    return dist.TransformedDistribution(base, transforms)

with torch.no_grad():
    centre = (lo + hi) / 2
    q_mu.copy_(torch.logit((centre - lo) / (hi - lo)))

print(f"Initial q centre (constrained): {build_q().sample().detach().cpu().numpy()}")

Now the objective:

def make_conditioning(theta_samples):
    fixed = torch.ones_like(theta_samples[:, 0])
    values = {
        "I_0": theta_samples[:, 0],
        "beta": theta_samples[:, 1],
        "gamma": theta_samples[:, 2],
        "omega": theta_samples[:, 3],
        "mu": TRUE_MU * fixed,
    }
    full_params = torch.stack(
        [values[name] for name in cfg.dataset.surrogate_input_variables],
        dim=1,
    )
    return (full_params - input_mean) / input_std


def compute_log_likelihood(y, theta_samples):
    n_mc = theta_samples.shape[0]
    full_params = make_conditioning(theta_samples)
    y_batch = y.expand(n_mc, -1, -1)

    z, total_logdet_scaled = nf(y_batch, full_params)

    log_pz = -0.5 * z.reshape(n_mc, -1).pow(2).sum(dim=1) \
             - 0.5 * DATA_DIM * math.log(2 * math.pi)
    true_logdet = DATA_DIM * total_logdet_scaled
    return log_pz + true_logdet


def compute_elbo(n_mc=32):
    q = build_q()
    theta_samples = q.rsample((n_mc,))
    theta_clamped = torch.stack([
        theta_samples[:, i].clamp(lo[i] + 1e-6, hi[i] - 1e-6)
        for i in range(n_params)
    ], dim=1)

    log_lik = compute_log_likelihood(y_obs, theta_clamped)
    log_q = q.log_prob(theta_clamped)
    log_prior = -torch.log(hi - lo).sum()

    return (log_lik + log_prior - log_q).mean()

Finally, we optimise

nf.eval()

vi_optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([q_mu, q_L_flat], lr=0.02)
n_vi_steps = 1500
n_mc = 32
elbo_history = []

for step in range(n_vi_steps):
    vi_optimizer.zero_grad()
    elbo = compute_elbo(n_mc=n_mc)
    (-elbo).backward()
    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_([q_mu, q_L_flat], max_norm=5.0)
    vi_optimizer.step()
    elbo_history.append(elbo.item())

    if step % 100 == 0 or step == n_vi_steps - 1:
        with torch.no_grad():
            q = build_q()
            mean_c = q.sample((1000,)).mean(dim=0)
        means = ", ".join(
            f"{name}={mean_c[i]:.4f}" for i, name in enumerate(PARAM_BOUNDS)
        )
        print(f"Step {step:4d}  ELBO={elbo.item():10.1f}  q_mean=[{means}]")

Now we plot the ELBO over time and the approximate posterior:

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(8, 3))
ax.plot(elbo_history, lw=0.5, alpha=0.4, label="ELBO")
window = 50
if len(elbo_history) > window:
    smoothed = np.convolve(elbo_history, np.ones(window) / window, mode="valid")
    ax.plot(np.arange(window - 1, len(elbo_history)), smoothed, lw=2, color="red",
            label=f"{window}-step moving avg")
ax.set(xlabel="VI step", ylabel="ELBO")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()

# Corner plot
with torch.no_grad():
    q_final = build_q()
    posterior_samples = q_final.sample((5000,)).cpu().numpy()

param_names = [r"$I_0$", r"$\beta$", r"$\gamma$", r"$\omega$"]
true_vals = [TRUE_I0, TRUE_BETA, TRUE_GAMMA, TRUE_OMEGA]
bounds = list(PARAM_BOUNDS.values())

fig2, axes2 = plt.subplots(n_params, n_params, figsize=(10, 10))
for i in range(n_params):
    for j in range(n_params):
        ax = axes2[i, j]
        if j > i:
            ax.axis("off")
            continue
        if i == j:
            ax.hist(posterior_samples[:, i], bins=50, density=True,
                    color="steelblue", alpha=0.7, edgecolor="none")
            ax.axvline(true_vals[i], color="red", lw=2, ls="--", label="True")
            ax.set_xlim(bounds[i])
            if i == 0:
                ax.legend(fontsize=8)
        else:
            ax.hist2d(posterior_samples[:, j], posterior_samples[:, i],
                      bins=40, cmap="Blues", density=True)
            ax.axvline(true_vals[j], color="red", lw=1, ls="--")
            ax.axhline(true_vals[i], color="red", lw=1, ls="--")
            ax.scatter([true_vals[j]], [true_vals[i]], color="red", s=30, zorder=5)
            ax.set_xlim(bounds[j])
            ax.set_ylim(bounds[i])
        if j == 0:
            ax.set_ylabel(param_names[i])
        if i == n_params - 1:
            ax.set_xlabel(param_names[j])

plt.suptitle(r"Approximate Posterior $q(I_0, \beta, \gamma, \omega \mid y_{obs})$", fontsize=13)
plt.tight_layout()

Final sanity check:

with torch.no_grad():
    q_final = build_q()
    theta_post = q_final.sample((10,))
    full_params_post = make_conditioning(theta_post)

    z_rand = torch.randn((10, *y_obs.shape[1:]), device=DEVICE)
    pp_samples, _ = nf.reverse(z_rand, full_params_post)
    pp_samples = pp_samples * series_std + series_mean
    pp_samples = pp_samples.clamp(min=0).cpu().numpy()

colors_pp = {"S": "#2E86AB", "I": "#C73E1D", "R": "#6A994E", "D": "#C21B8A"}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(12, 4.5))
for s in range(pp_samples.shape[0]):
    for j, (label, color) in enumerate(colors_pp.items()):
        ax.plot(pp_samples[s, :, j], color=color, alpha=0.6, lw=0.8)

for j, (label, color) in enumerate(colors_pp.items()):
    ax.plot(y_obs_raw[:, j], color=color, lw=2.5, ls="--", label=f"{label} (observed)")

ax.set(xlabel="time (days)", ylabel="count", title="Posterior Predictive Check")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()

print("=" * 60)
print("Variational Inference Results")
print("=" * 60)
with torch.no_grad():
    vi_samples = q_final.sample((10000,)).cpu().numpy()
for i, (name, true_val) in enumerate(zip(PARAM_BOUNDS, true_vals)):
    mean = vi_samples[:, i].mean()
    std = vi_samples[:, i].std()
    q025 = np.percentile(vi_samples[:, i], 2.5)
    q975 = np.percentile(vi_samples[:, i], 97.5)
    print(f"  {name:6s}: mean={mean:.4f} +/- {std:.4f}  "
          f"95% CI=[{q025:.4f}, {q975:.4f}]  true={true_val:.4f}  "
          f"{'OK' if q025 <= true_val <= q975 else 'MISS'}")

title: VI and MCMC with iTarFlow
text:
MCMC
We can also sample from the same surrogate-based posterior using Pyro’s No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS), an adaptive Hamiltonian Monte Carlo method. We reuse the uniform priors, observation, and compute_log_likelihood above; the mortality rate remains fixed.
Pyro is optional. Install it into the project’s environment before continuing (the package is named pyro-ppl, but imported as pyro):

%%bash
uv pip install pyro-ppl

Each pyro.sample declares a parameter’s prior. pyro.factor adds the surrogate log-likelihood to the joint log density. Pyro handles the transforms between bounded parameters and the unconstrained space used by NUTS. Keep gradients enabled through the surrogate, just as for VI.

import pyro
import pyro.distributions as pyro_dist
from pyro.infer import MCMC, NUTS

pyro.set_rng_seed(42)

def posterior_model():
    theta = torch.stack([
        pyro.sample(name, pyro_dist.Uniform(lo[i], hi[i]))
        for i, name in enumerate(PARAM_BOUNDS)
    ])
    log_lik = compute_log_likelihood(y_obs, theta.unsqueeze(0))[0]
    pyro.factor("surrogate_likelihood", log_lik)

Warmup adapts the step size and mass matrix, and its draws are discarded. We use a full mass matrix to accommodate correlations between the parameters. This example runs one chain for straightforward notebook execution.

kernel = NUTS(posterior_model, full_mass=True, target_accept_prob=0.8)
mcmc = MCMC(kernel, warmup_steps=500, num_samples=1000, num_chains=1)
mcmc.run()
mcmc.summary(prob=0.95)

mcmc_draws = mcmc.get_samples()
theta_mcmc = torch.stack([mcmc_draws[name] for name in PARAM_BOUNDS], dim=1)
mcmc_samples = theta_mcmc.detach().cpu().numpy()

Inspect the effective sample sizes, divergences, and trace plots before interpreting the posterior. The single-chain summary uses a split-chain R-hat; it does not replace checking agreement across independently initialized chains. Increase warmup or sampling length if mixing is poor.

MCMC trace plots
Plot the retained MCMC draws in sampling order to inspect mixing. Dashed lines mark the true parameter values.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(n_params, 1, figsize=(10, 2.5 * n_params), sharex=True)
for i, name in enumerate(PARAM_BOUNDS):
    axes[i].plot(mcmc_samples[:, i], lw=0.6)
    axes[i].axhline(true_vals[i], color="red", ls="--", label="True")
    axes[i].set(ylabel=param_names[i])
axes[-1].set_xlabel("MCMC draw")
axes[0].legend()
plt.tight_layout()



MCMC posterior predictive check
Finally, draw trajectories conditional on samples from the MCMC posterior, using the same conditioning and inverse normalization as for VI.

with torch.no_grad():
    selected = torch.randperm(theta_mcmc.shape[0], device=theta_mcmc.device)[:10]
    conditioning = make_conditioning(theta_mcmc[selected])
    z_rand = torch.randn((len(selected), *y_obs.shape[1:]), device=DEVICE)
    mcmc_pp, _ = nf.reverse(z_rand, conditioning)
    mcmc_pp = (mcmc_pp * series_std + series_mean).clamp(min=0).cpu().numpy()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 4.5))
for sample in mcmc_pp:
    for j, (label, color) in enumerate(colors_pp.items()):
        ax.plot(sample[:, j], color=color, alpha=0.6, lw=0.8)
for j, (label, color) in enumerate(colors_pp.items()):
    ax.plot(y_obs_raw[:, j], color=color, lw=2.5, ls="--", label=f"{label} (observed)")
ax.set(xlabel="time (days)", ylabel="count", title="MCMC Posterior Predictive Check")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()



VI and MCMC posterior comparison
Overlay the marginal densities on the diagonal and joint samples below it to compare both uncertainty and correlations. The joint panels show an equal number of draws from each method; dashed lines mark the true parameters.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(n_params, n_params, figsize=(10, 10))
comparison_samples = [("VI", posterior_samples, "steelblue"),
                      ("MCMC", mcmc_samples, "darkorange")]
n_show = min(1000, len(posterior_samples), len(mcmc_samples))
for i in range(n_params):
    for j in range(n_params):
        ax = axes[i, j]
        if j > i:
            ax.axis("off")
            continue
        if i == j:
            bins = np.linspace(*bounds[i], 60)
            for label, samples, color in comparison_samples:
                ax.hist(samples[:, i], bins=bins, density=True,
                        histtype="step", lw=1.8, color=color, label=label)
            ax.axvline(true_vals[i], color="black", ls="--", label="True")
            ax.set_xlim(bounds[i])
        else:
            for label, samples, color in comparison_samples:
                ax.scatter(samples[:n_show, j], samples[:n_show, i],
                           s=5, alpha=0.15, color=color, rasterized=True)
            ax.axvline(true_vals[j], color="black", ls="--", lw=1)
            ax.axhline(true_vals[i], color="black", ls="--", lw=1)
            ax.set_xlim(bounds[j])
            ax.set_ylim(bounds[i])
        if j == 0:
            ax.set_ylabel("Density" if i == 0 else param_names[i])
        if i == n_params - 1:
            ax.set_xlabel(param_names[j])
axes[0, 0].legend()
fig.suptitle("VI and MCMC posterior comparison")
plt.tight_layout()
